title: What Is Frontend Development?
description: Discover what frontend engineers actually build, what happens in the browser, and why frontend is much more than making a website look nice.
mastery: Learner can explain frontend development in plain language, identify real frontend responsibilities, distinguish frontend work from design and backend work, and explain the basic roles of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript using a concrete example.
learningObjectives: Define frontend development in plain language without relying on memorized technology names.
Identify at least three responsibilities of a frontend engineer in a real web application.
Distinguish frontend engineering from visual design and backend engineering using concrete examples.
Explain the basic roles of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript in a browser-based interface.

sections.text: Welcome to the Frontend

When you open a website, the things you can see, click, type into, scroll through, and interact with are part of the frontend experience. The page you're reading, the button you're about to press, the form checking your input, and the interface changing when you click something are all things frontend engineers help build.

Frontend development is the practice of building the browser-facing part of a website or web application: its structure, presentation, interaction, and browser-side behavior. It is where software meets the person using it.

A useful beginner mental model: if the user is directly experiencing it in the browser, frontend engineering is probably involved. The exact boundary gets more nuanced later, but this model gives you a solid starting map.
Frontend Is Not Just 'Making It Pretty'

A visual designer and a frontend engineer may work closely together, but they solve different problems. A designer may decide how a button should look, how information should be arranged, or how an interaction should feel. The frontend engineer turns those ideas and requirements into working software that behaves correctly on real browsers, devices, input methods, and data.

Frontend engineers also deal with problems that a design mockup cannot solve by itself: what happens when data is loading, what happens when something fails, how the interface responds to keyboard input, how it behaves on a small screen, and what the browser should do when the user interacts with it.

Beginner trap: thinking frontend means CSS with a fancy job title. CSS matters a lot, but frontend engineering also includes structure, behavior, browser logic, accessibility, responsive behavior, debugging, and data-driven interfaces. Your button can look absolutely magnificent and still do nothing. The browser will not be impressed.
Frontend vs Backend

The backend usually handles work that happens away from the user's browser, such as storing data, applying business rules, authenticating users, communicating with databases, and responding to requests. The frontend handles the browser-facing experience and communicates with backend systems when it needs data or server-side work.

Imagine a user changing their profile name. The frontend can display the form, validate obvious input, show a loading state, disable the Save button while a request is being processed, and tell the user whether the operation succeeded. A backend may verify the user, apply business rules, store the new value, and send back a response.

sections.title: The boundary is useful, not absolute
sections.subtitle: A beginner model you will refine later
sections.content: Modern web applications can blur the frontend/backend boundary. Some frameworks execute code on both the server and the client, and some applications move more work between them depending on the problem being solved. For now, think in terms of responsibility: frontend code primarily creates and manages the experience in the browser; backend systems primarily provide server-side data, rules, and services that support it.

sections.text: The Three Foundation Technologies
Forge starts with three core web technologies: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. They have different jobs, but they work together.
HTML gives the page structure and meaning. In this example, it creates a button that the browser understands as a button.

sections.title: CSS — Presentation

sections.text: CSS controls presentation: colors, spacing, sizing, borders, layout, typography, and many other visual properties.

sections.title: JavaScript — Behavior

sections.text: JavaScript can make the interface respond to what the user does. Here, clicking the button changes its state and text. You do not need to understand every line yet. The important idea is that JavaScript can add behavior and logic to the page.
Remember the beginner model: HTML gives the page structure, CSS gives it presentation, and JavaScript gives it behavior. You will learn where this model gets more interesting as Forge goes deeper.
See Frontend in the Real World

Pick a website you already use. Look at one thing you can see, one thing you can interact with, and one thing that changes after you interact with it. You are already looking at frontend engineering—you just have not been calling it that yet.

sections.title: One User Action, Multiple Responsibilities
sections.description: A user clicks Save → the frontend responds immediately to the interaction → the frontend may send data to a backend → the backend processes and stores the data → a response returns → the frontend updates the interface for the user.

sections.text: Practice: Become a Frontend Detective

Choose one website or web app you use often. Find one example of structure, one example of presentation, and one example of behavior. Then find one thing that probably depends on backend work behind the scenes. Finally, explain what frontend development means in your own words without simply repeating the words 'HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.'

sections.label: Explain frontend development in your own words. Then give one example of frontend work, one example of backend work, and one example of design work from a real website or app you use.
sections.hint: Think about what the user directly interacts with, what happens behind the scenes, and what someone might decide before the code is written.

sections.text: Forge Check
Before moving on, try this without looking back: if someone handed you a button that looks perfect but does absolutely nothing, which part of frontend development would you need to investigate first?
If your answer is that appearance alone is not enough and the interface also needs behavior, you have the core idea. The browser is about to become a lot less mysterious.

exercises.title: Frontend Detective
exercises.brief: Choose one website or web app you use regularly. Identify one example of structure, one example of presentation, one example of behavior, and one example of something that likely depends on backend work. Then explain frontend development in two or three sentences without using HTML, CSS, or JavaScript as your definition.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes frontend development?
options: Building and managing only the database and server infrastructure behind an application.
Designing visual mockups without implementing them as working software.
Building and managing the browser-facing structure, presentation, interaction, and behavior of a web experience.
Managing only domain names, DNS records, and hosting accounts.
quiz.explanation: Frontend development focuses on the part of the application users directly experience in the browser, including structure, presentation, interaction, and browser-side behavior.

quiz.question: Which example is primarily frontend behavior?
options: A button has rounded corners.
A page contains a main heading and a navigation region.
A button becomes disabled after the user clicks it.
A database stores the user's profile information.
quiz.explanation: A button changing state in response to a user interaction is behavior handled by frontend code. Rounded corners and page structure are presentation and structure, while storing profile information is generally backend work.

quiz.question: A designer creates a mockup for a checkout page and a frontend engineer turns it into a working page that handles real user input. What best describes the relationship?
options: The designer and frontend engineer are doing exactly the same job.
The designer plans the visual experience while the frontend engineer implements the working interface and its browser-side behavior.
The frontend engineer only changes colors and fonts after the designer is finished.
The frontend engineer is responsible only for sending data to the database.
quiz.explanation: Design and frontend engineering overlap, but they solve different parts of the product problem. The designer may define the visual experience while the frontend engineer turns that direction into functioning software.

summary: Frontend development is the work of building the browser-facing part of a web application: structure, presentation, interaction, and browser-side behavior. HTML provides structure, CSS provides presentation, and JavaScript can provide behavior. Frontend engineering works alongside design and backend systems but is not the same discipline as either.

title: How the Web Works
description: Build a simple mental model of how a browser and a server communicate so a webpage can appear on your screen.
mastery: Learner can explain the basic client-server request/response cycle in their own words, identify the roles of the browser and server, and trace the basic flow of a webpage request from client to server and back.
learningObjectives: Explain the basic client-server model used by the web.
Describe what a browser sends to a server and what the server sends back.
Distinguish a webpage loaded from the web from a local file opened on the user's device.
Trace a simple request/response exchange using the terms client, server, request, and response.

sections.text: The Web Is a Conversation

When you type a website address into your browser and a page appears, it can feel like the browser simply opened a file. That is not what is happening. For a typical web request, your browser asks another computer for something, and that computer sends something back. The browser and the server are having a conversation.

The browser is usually the client: it is the software making the request on your behalf. The server is the system that receives the request and sends back the requested resource or a response describing what happened.

A useful mental model: client asks, server answers. It is a little like ordering food. You place the order, the kitchen receives it, the kitchen prepares something, and something comes back to your table. The browser is not ordering jollof rice, but the pattern is surprisingly similar.
Client and Server

In a web application, the client is commonly your browser running on your phone, laptop, or another device. It is responsible for requesting resources, receiving responses, and using those responses to build the experience you see and interact with.

A server is a computer or service that listens for requests and responds to them. Depending on the application, it may return HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, JSON data, or another kind of resource. It may also perform work before responding, such as checking permissions, reading data, or applying business rules.

sections.title: The Basic Web Conversation
sections.description: 1. The client (browser) asks for a resource. 2. The request travels across a network. 3. A server receives the request. 4. The server prepares or retrieves the requested resource. 5. The server sends a response back. 6. The browser receives the response and uses it to continue the user experience.

sections.text: Request In, Response Out

A request is a message sent by the client asking a server to do something or provide something. A response is the server's answer. The exact contents become much more interesting later, but the basic pattern is simple: request goes out, response comes back.

sections.title: A simplified HTTP exchange
sections.code:
REQUEST GET /products HTTP/1.1 Host: example.com RESPONSE HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type: text/html

Products

sections.text: The request is asking for the /products resource from example.com. The response begins by telling the client what happened. A 200 status means the request succeeded, and the response then contains information and content the browser can use.

sections.title: So is the server just a computer with a website folder on it?
sections.subtitle: Useful beginner model, but there is more happening
sections.content: Sometimes a server really is serving a static file. Other times it is running application code, querying a database, checking authentication, calling another service, or generating a response dynamically. The important beginner idea is not that every server works the same way. It is that the client requests something and the server is responsible for handling that request and producing a response.

sections.text: Why the First Load Needs the Network

If a website is not already available locally, the browser needs to communicate with the systems that can provide its resources. Without that exchange, the browser does not magically possess the site's latest HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, or data.

Common misconception: 'The internet is just where websites live.' Not quite. The internet is the network that lets systems communicate. Your browser uses that network to reach servers and exchange data with them.
What Happens After the Response?

Receiving a response is not necessarily the end of the story. A response can contain HTML that causes the browser to request additional CSS, JavaScript, fonts, images, and other resources. The browser then processes what it receives and builds the interface you eventually see.

That means the page appearing on your screen is the result of a chain of work, not a single magical file-opening event. The next lesson will trace that chain more closely, from a URL to DNS, a request, a response, and finally a rendered page.
Practice: Find the Conversation

Think about an action you performed online today: loading a news article, refreshing a social feed, checking your bank balance, or opening a new page in a shopping app. Identify the client, describe what the client was asking for, and describe what the server needed to send back for the action to work.

sections.title: Client or Server?
sections.instructions: For each action, decide whether it primarily belongs to the client or server side. Try answering before revealing the explanation. Then change an example and predict which side is responsible.

sections.label: Explain the client-server model without looking at the lesson. Use one real example and identify the client, the request, the server, and the response.
sections.hint: Think: Who asks? What are they asking for? Who answers? What comes back?

sections.text: Forge Check

Imagine you are sitting in a café and open a website you have never visited before. Your browser shows a loading indicator. Before the page can appear, something has to travel away from your device and something has to come back. That simple exchange is one of the foundations of everything you are about to build.

exercises.title: Trace a Simple Request
exercises.brief: Choose one website or web app you used today. Write four short lines: Client, Request, Server, Response. Describe what each one means for the action you performed. Then explain in one sentence why the client and server need a network connection to communicate.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the basic relationship between a browser and a server?
options: The browser asks the server for resources, and the server responds.
The server asks the browser for resources, and the browser responds.
The browser and server are the same thing running on different screens.
The browser only communicates with a server after the page has already loaded.
quiz.explanation: In the basic client-server model, the browser acts as the client and can send requests to a server. The server processes those requests and sends back responses.

quiz.question: Which of the following is most likely part of a server's responsibility?
options: Applying a button's hover color in the browser
Displaying the final pixels on the user's screen
Storing application data and responding to requests for that data
Detecting when the user moves a mouse over a button
quiz.explanation: Servers commonly handle data storage and server-side processing. The browser is responsible for the direct user interface and browser-side interactions.

quiz.question: Why can a page sometimes continue responding briefly after the network connection disappears?
options: The browser can never need the network after the first request.
The browser may already have the resources and code it needs locally in memory or cache.
The server moves into the user's computer when the connection drops.
HTML automatically recreates missing network connections.
quiz.explanation: Once resources and application code have already been loaded, the browser may continue running them locally even if the network becomes unavailable. New network-dependent actions can still fail.

summary: The web works through communication between clients and servers. A browser commonly acts as the client: it sends requests across a network, and servers respond with resources or data. The browser then uses those responses to build and run the experience the user sees.
interviewQuestions: What is the client-server model?

Why is understanding client-server communication useful to a frontend engineer when debugging an application?

title: What Happens When You Click a Link?
description: Trace what happens between a click and a rendered page, from the URL and DNS lookup to the server response and browser rendering.
mastery: Learner can explain the major stages of a web navigation in the correct order, describe the role of DNS, distinguish the HTTP request from the server response, and trace the journey of a new URL from user action to browser rendering.
learningObjectives: Describe the major stages that occur when a user navigates to a new URL.
Explain what DNS does and why a hostname must be resolved before the browser can normally contact the destination server.
Distinguish an HTTP request from an HTTP response and identify what each contains at a high level.
Explain how the browser uses the returned resources to begin rendering the page.

sections.text: The Journey Behind One Click

Clicking a link feels instantaneous. You click, the old page disappears, and the new one shows up. Underneath that tiny action, however, the browser has several jobs to do before it can show you the destination.

For a simple mental model, think of the journey like this: the browser figures out where it needs to go, finds the destination, sends a request, receives a response, and starts turning the returned resources into a page. The real browser process contains more detail and sometimes happens in parallel, but this sequence gives you the map you need before we add the machinery.

A useful interview mental model is: URL → DNS → connection → HTTP request → response → browser work. You do not need to sound like a networking textbook. You do need to know what problem each stage solves.

steps.title: 1. The browser gets the destination
steps.description: You click a link such as https://example.com/products. The browser now knows the URL it needs to navigate to and can determine the hostname, path, and other parts of the address.

steps.title: 2. DNS helps find the destination
steps.description: The hostname example.com is a human-friendly name. DNS, the Domain Name System, helps resolve that hostname to an IP address the network can use. Browsers and operating systems may already have a cached answer, so a DNS lookup does not necessarily mean starting from scratch every time.

steps.title: 3. The browser establishes communication
steps.description: The browser needs a usable network connection to the destination. For an HTTPS page, this includes the security setup needed to communicate securely. You do not need to memorize the lower-level networking details yet; the important idea is that the browser prepares a path for the request.

steps.title: 4. The browser sends an HTTP request
steps.description: The browser sends an HTTP request asking the server for the requested resource. For example, it might send a GET request for /products.

steps.title: 5. The server sends an HTTP response
steps.description: The server receives the request, performs whatever work is necessary, and sends back a response. That response includes a status and may contain HTML, data, or information that tells the browser what kind of content it is receiving.

steps.title: 6. The browser starts building the experience
steps.description: The browser processes the response and begins building the page. HTML can lead to requests for CSS, JavaScript, images, fonts, and other resources. The browser parses what it receives, applies styles, runs JavaScript when appropriate, and eventually paints the interface to the screen.

sections.text: Common mistake: saying 'I clicked the link and the server rendered the page.' For a typical browser experience, the server sends resources or generated content, while the browser does substantial work to parse those resources, run client-side code, calculate layout, and paint what you see.
What Is DNS Actually Doing?

Imagine trying to call someone when you know their name but not their phone number. DNS plays a similar role for domain names. Humans prefer names like example.com; network communication ultimately needs an address that can be routed to.

So when the browser needs to reach example.com, DNS helps answer a question like: 'What address should I use for this hostname?' Once the browser has a usable address, it can continue with the network connection and request.

sections.title: Does DNS always happen every time I click a link?
sections.subtitle: Not necessarily
sections.content: No. DNS information can be cached by the browser, operating system, local network, or other infrastructure. Connections can also be reused. That is why a real browser's behavior is more complicated than 'click → DNS lookup every single time.' The simplified sequence is still useful because it teaches the role DNS plays when the destination needs to be resolved.

sections.text: Request vs Response

sections.title: A simplified HTTP exchange
sections.code:
REQUEST GET /products HTTP/1.1 Host: example.com RESPONSE HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type: text/html

Products

sections.text: The request says what the client wants. Here, GET asks for the /products resource. The response says what happened and returns content or other information. A 200 status means the server is reporting success for that request.

This is where your previous lesson's request/response model becomes practical. The browser is no longer just 'asking a server for a page' in the abstract. You can now point to the name-resolution step, the request, the response, and the browser work that follows.
Then the Browser Gets Busy

Receiving HTML does not mean the browser is finished. The HTML may reference stylesheets, scripts, images, fonts, and other resources. The browser can make additional requests for those resources while continuing the work of building the page.

sections.title: Navigation at a Glance
sections.description: User click → URL identified → hostname resolved when needed → connection established → HTTP request sent → server response received → browser processes resources → layout/style/script work → pixels appear on screen.

sections.text: Practice: Be the Browser

Pick a website you have never opened before. Imagine you typed its URL and pressed Enter. Before moving on, try to say the sequence out loud without looking: destination, DNS, connection, request, response, browser processing. Then explain what DNS contributed and what the browser did after receiving the response.

sections.title: Trace the Request Lifecycle
sections.instructions: The stages are hidden behind a step-by-step simulation. Before revealing each stage, predict what the browser does next. Pay attention to the difference between finding the destination, sending a request, receiving a response, and rendering the result.

sections.label: Without looking at the lesson, explain what happens when you enter https://example.com/products and press Enter. Include the role of DNS, the HTTP request, the server response, and the browser's rendering work.
sections.hint: Start with the URL. Then ask: how does the browser know where to go, what does it request, what comes back, and what does the browser do with it?

sections.text: Forge Check

You are now carrying a useful debugging map. When a page fails to appear, you do not have to stare at the spinner and hope it develops a personality. You can ask: Did the destination resolve? Did the request leave? Did the server respond? Did the browser receive and process what came back?
In the next lesson, we will separate the browser, client, and server roles more carefully so you can reason about where different pieces of web behavior actually happen.

exercises.title: Explain the Journey
exercises.brief: Choose an unfamiliar website or URL and write a six-step explanation of what happens from pressing Enter to seeing the page. Include URL identification, DNS when needed, connection, HTTP request, server response, and browser processing. Then explain which step would be most likely to involve DNS caching.

quiz.question: What is the main job of DNS in a typical web navigation?
options: It renders HTML into pixels on the screen.
It translates a hostname such as example.com into an address the network can use.
It sends the final HTML response to the browser.
It stores the user's browser history.
quiz.explanation: DNS helps resolve human-readable hostnames to IP addresses or other address information that networking systems can use to reach the destination.

quiz.question: Which statement correctly separates an HTTP request from an HTTP response?
options: The request is sent by the client asking for something; the response is the server's reply.
The request is always sent by the server; the response is always sent by the browser.
The request contains only CSS; the response contains only HTML.
The request happens after rendering; the response happens before the user clicks anything.
quiz.explanation: The client sends the HTTP request, and the server sends an HTTP response. Both messages can contain more than one kind of data, so they are not limited to CSS or HTML.

quiz.question: Why might a browser make additional requests after receiving the first HTML response?
options: The HTML may reference resources such as CSS, JavaScript, images, or fonts that the browser also needs.
The browser always sends the same request twice by mistake.
DNS requires the browser to download a second copy of the webpage.
The server cannot send HTML unless the browser first renders an empty page.
quiz.explanation: HTML can reference additional resources. The browser can discover those references while parsing the document and request the resources needed to continue building the page.

summary: When a user navigates to a new URL, the browser identifies the destination, resolves the hostname when necessary, establishes the required connection, sends an HTTP request, receives a server response, and processes the returned resources to build and render the page. The real browser pipeline is more complex and can involve caching, connection reuse, parallel requests, and other optimizations, but this sequence provides the essential mental model.
interviewQuestions: What happens when you type a URL into a browser and press Enter?
What is DNS and why does a browser need it?
What is the difference between an HTTP request and an HTTP response?
After receiving HTML, why might the browser make additional network requests?

title: Browser, Server, and Client
description: Understand where responsibility lives between the browser and the server, and why frontend engineers need to reason about both sides.
mastery: Learner can explain the browser/client and server distinction in their own words, identify which side is responsible for common web tasks, and explain why important persistent data and business rules cannot safely depend on the browser alone.
learningObjectives: Explain why a browser is commonly considered the client in a web application.
Identify common responsibilities handled by the browser and common responsibilities handled by a server.
Explain why persistent data, authentication, authorization, and important business rules must not rely solely on client-side code.
Distinguish temporary browser state from durable server-side data using real examples.

sections.text: Two Sides of the Same Application

In the last lesson, you followed a request from a browser to a server and watched a response come back. Now let's zoom in. What exactly is the browser responsible for? What belongs on the server? And why should a frontend engineer care about the server if their code mostly runs in the browser?

The short version is this: the browser is where the user experiences the application, while the server is where systems can provide shared data, enforce rules, and perform work that should not be trusted to the user's device.

Think of a restaurant. The browser is the dining room where the customer sees the menu, places an order, and interacts with the staff. The server is much closer to the kitchen and the systems that actually manage the ingredients, orders, and rules. You can redesign the menu from the dining room; you probably should not let the customer rewrite the inventory database.
The Browser Is the Client

In web development, the browser is commonly called the client because it is the software making requests and presenting the resulting experience to the user. It downloads and processes HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, responds to user input, manages browser-side state, and renders the interface.

That means a surprising amount of work happens on the user's own device. When you click a button, type into a form, open a menu, drag an item, or see an animation, the browser is doing work locally. The user's laptop or phone is not merely a glass window looking at a website. It is actively running the frontend application.

Common misconception: the browser is just displaying whatever the server sends. Nope. The browser is doing a lot of work after the response arrives. It parses documents, applies styles, runs JavaScript, handles interactions, manages temporary state, and turns all of that into the interface you see.
What the Server Is Responsible For

A server usually handles work that needs to be shared, trusted, persistent, or protected. It may read and write data, authenticate users, enforce permissions, apply business rules, communicate with databases, and respond to requests from many different clients.

Imagine an online store. The browser can show you a shopping cart and calculate what the current items add up to for a smooth user experience. But the server still needs to be the trusted authority for things such as inventory, account permissions, order records, and the final rules for what a user is allowed to purchase.

sections.title: Who Is Responsible for What?
sections.description: Browser / Client: renders the interface, handles user interaction, runs frontend JavaScript, manages temporary UI state, and requests data. Server: stores durable data, applies business rules, authenticates and authorizes users, communicates with databases and services, and responds to client requests.

sections.text: Temporary State vs Durable Data

One useful distinction is temporary state versus durable data. The browser can keep temporary information such as whether a menu is open, which tab is selected, or what a user has typed into a form. That state may disappear when the page is refreshed, the tab is closed, or the application resets it.

Durable data is information that needs to remain correct and available beyond one browser session: an account balance, an order, a saved profile, an inventory count, or a permission. That kind of information normally belongs behind a server and a persistent data store.

sections.title: Why can't the browser just be trusted?
sections.subtitle: Because the user controls the browser
sections.content: Code running in the browser is running on a device the user controls. A user can inspect it, modify requests, change client-side state, disable JavaScript, or interact with the application in ways the original developer did not expect. Client-side validation is excellent for user experience, but it is not a security boundary. Important authorization checks and business rules must be enforced on systems the user does not control.

sections.text: Important rule: never treat the browser as the final authority for sensitive decisions. A button being hidden does not mean an operation is forbidden. A client-side 'admin' check does not make someone an admin. The server must enforce rules that actually matter.
A Real Example: Logging In

Suppose you enter an email and password into a login form. The browser can validate that the fields are not empty, show loading feedback, and display an error message if the request fails. But it should not decide by itself that the password is correct. The server receives the credentials or authentication request, verifies the user through the appropriate authentication system, and decides whether access should be granted.

This is why frontend engineers need to understand backend responsibilities even when they are not writing the backend code. The interface is only one half of the conversation. A frontend engineer who understands both sides can reason about failures, security, data flow, and user experience much more effectively.
Browser and Client Are Not Perfect Synonyms

In frontend conversations, people often use browser and client almost interchangeably because the browser is usually the software acting as the client. But technically, a client is any software that makes a request to a service. A mobile app, desktop application, command-line program, or another server can also be a client.
Easy memory trick: 'client' describes the role; 'browser' describes one common kind of software playing that role. The browser is a client. The client is not always a browser.
Practice: Pick a Side

For each situation below, decide whether the responsibility primarily belongs to the browser, the server, or both. Then explain why: showing a dropdown menu, storing an account balance, checking whether a user is allowed to delete a post, displaying a loading spinner, saving a new profile name, and validating that an email field looks correctly formatted.

sections.label: Explain the difference between the browser/client and the server in your own words. Then give two browser responsibilities, two server responsibilities, and one example of work that involves both sides.
sections.hint: Think about where the user interacts, where durable data lives, where important rules are enforced, and where requests begin.

sections.text: Forge Check

A user clicks 'Delete Account' and the frontend hides the button for ordinary users. Does that alone make the account impossible to delete? No. The browser can control the interface, but the server must enforce the actual permission. That's the distinction you want to remember.

You now have the basic map: the browser is the user's side of the application, the server is the trusted system behind it, and requests connect the two. One lesson remains in this first module—and this time, we're going to turn that map around and look at Forge itself.

exercises.title: Browser, Server, or Both?
exercises.brief: Classify six real application responsibilities as browser, server, or both: opening a menu, storing a profile name, checking permissions, showing a loading state, saving a profile change, and validating an email field. For each answer, give one sentence explaining why.

quiz.question: Why is a browser commonly called a client?
options: Because it is responsible for physically hosting every website.
Because it is software that requests resources and services and presents the resulting experience to the user.
Because browsers permanently store all application data.
Because only browsers are capable of sending HTTP requests.
quiz.explanation: A client is software that requests resources or services. A browser commonly plays that role when it communicates with web servers.

quiz.question: Which responsibility should primarily be enforced on the server rather than trusted to the browser?
options: Whether a navigation menu is currently open.
Whether a button changes color after being clicked.
Whether a user is authorized to delete another user's account.
Whether a loading spinner is visible while a request is in progress.
quiz.explanation: Authorization is a security-sensitive rule. The browser can improve the user experience by hiding or disabling controls, but the server must enforce whether the operation is actually allowed.

quiz.question: Which statement best distinguishes the browser from the term 'client'?
options: A browser is one type of software that can act as a client; a client is a broader role.
A client is always a browser.
A browser can only display content and cannot make requests.
The terms always mean exactly the same thing in every technical context.
quiz.explanation: Browser and client are often used interchangeably in frontend conversations, but technically a client is any software taking the client role in communication with a service. Browsers are one common example.

summary: The browser commonly acts as the client: it renders the interface, runs frontend JavaScript, handles user interaction, and makes requests. Servers handle shared and durable responsibilities such as data storage, authentication, authorization, and business rules. The browser can improve user experience, but important rules and persistent data must not depend on trusting the client.
interviewQuestions: What is the difference between a browser and a client?
Which responsibilities should belong on the server rather than being trusted to the browser, and why?
Why is client-side validation useful even though it cannot replace server-side validation?
Give an example of a feature where both the browser and server have distinct responsibilities.

title: How Forge Works
description: Learn how Forge turns lessons into practice, feedback, and measurable progress so you can use the academy actively instead of treating it like a video library.
mastery: Learner can navigate Forge's core Learn, Practice, and Grow areas, identify where to learn a concept, where to practice it, and where to review progress and mastery.
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose of Forge's Learn, Practice, and Grow loop in plain language.
Identify where to read lessons and find curriculum content in Forge.
Identify the appropriate Forge area for practicing, debugging, building, and reviewing progress.
Complete a simple first-use navigation task across the core Forge learning surfaces.

sections.text: Welcome to Forge

You now know what frontend development is, how browsers and servers communicate, and where responsibility generally lives on each side. Before you start building, there is one more thing to understand: how to use the environment that is going to help you learn all of this.

Forge is designed around a simple idea: reading about a skill is only the beginning. You learn the concept, practice it, get feedback, revisit weak areas, and gradually become able to use the skill without being guided.
Think of Forge less like a bookshelf and more like a gym for frontend engineering. A bookshelf can explain how push-ups work. It cannot make your arms stronger. The practice part still has to happen.
The Learn → Practice → Grow Loop
Forge organizes your learning around three connected activities: Learn, Practice, and Grow.

sections.title: The Forge Learning Loop
sections.description: Learn → understand a concept and build a mental model → Practice → apply, build, debug, or explain the skill → Grow → review performance, mastery, weak areas, and progress → return to Practice or Learn where needed.

sections.text: 1. Learn
The Learn area is where you move through the curriculum. It contains the roadmap, modules, topics, and lessons that take you from the foundations of the web toward professional frontend engineering.

A lesson is where a concept is taught. It may include explanations, examples, code, diagrams, checkpoints, quizzes, and practical activities. The important part is that a lesson gives you something to understand, not just something to scroll past.
Do not race through lessons just to make the progress bar look impressive. The progress bar does not need a motivational speech. Your future debugging skills do.
2. Practice
Practice is where the information starts becoming a skill. Depending on what you are learning, Forge can send you into different practice surfaces.

The Playground is for experimenting with and building code. Debug Lab is for finding and fixing broken code. Whiteboard Mode is for planning flows, component relationships, layout ideas, and architecture. Projects are for combining multiple skills into something larger. Quizzes and Flashcards help with retrieval and reinforcement, while Daily Challenges provide short, repeated practice.

sections.title: Why so many practice surfaces?
sections.subtitle: Because 'I read it' and 'I can do it' are different achievements
sections.content: Different skills need different forms of practice. A concept may need retrieval practice. A coding skill needs implementation. A debugging skill needs broken software. Architecture benefits from diagrams and tradeoff discussions. Forge uses different surfaces so practice matches the skill instead of forcing every problem into the same format.

sections.text: 3. Grow

Grow is where you see what is happening to your skills over time. It is not simply a page that says how many lessons you clicked through. It is where Forge can surface progress, mastery, review needs, interview readiness, project progress, and other evidence of growth.
The goal is not to keep every number green at all times. The goal is to know what you can do confidently, what still needs practice, and where to spend your next useful hour.

A common mistake is treating completion as mastery. Finishing a lesson means you reached the end of the lesson. Mastery means the skill is becoming something you can use independently. Those are related, but they are not the same thing.
Where Everything Lives

steps.title: Start in Learn
steps.description: Use the Academy Roadmap to understand where you are going, then open Modules, Topics, and Lessons to find the specific concept you need to study.

steps.title: Move into Practice
steps.description: After learning something, use the practice area that matches the skill. Build in the Playground, investigate bugs in Debug Lab, plan ideas in Whiteboard Mode, and combine skills in Projects.

steps.title: Check your growth
steps.description: Use the Grow area to review mastery, progress, interview preparation, journal entries, certificates, and other evidence of your development.

steps.title: Return when something is weak
steps.description: If practice exposes a gap, do not treat that as failure. Return to the relevant lesson, review the concept, and practice again. That feedback loop is part of the system.

sections.text: Your First Mission

Now do a quick tour yourself. Find the Academy Roadmap. Find the Lesson Catalog. Find the Playground. Find Debug Lab. Find Whiteboard Mode. Then find the area where your overall progress and mastery are shown.

sections.title: Choose the Right Forge Tool
sections.instructions: Read each scenario and decide which Forge surface you would use. Reveal the explanation only after making your choice.

sections.text: Your First Forge Check

Without looking back, answer these in your own words: Where do you learn a new concept? Where would you practice writing code? Where would you investigate a bug? Where would you plan an architecture idea? Where would you look to understand your progress and mastery?

sections.label: Navigate to the Academy Roadmap, Lesson Catalog, Playground, Debug Lab, Whiteboard Mode, and Grow area. Then explain the purpose of Learn, Practice, and Grow in your own words.
sections.hint: Learn teaches the idea. Practice turns the idea into a skill. Grow helps you understand what is improving and what still needs work.

sections.text: One Last Thing

You are not expected to master Forge before you start learning frontend engineering. You only need to know where to go next. The academy will introduce the tools again when they become relevant, and your job is to actually use them.
The winning loop is simple: Learn something. Try it. Get stuck. Debug it. Try again. Explain it. Come back later. Repeat. That is how 'I think I understand this' slowly becomes 'give me the problem.'
You have finished the orientation. Next, we leave the tour behind and start building your understanding of the tools developers use to see what the browser is actually doing.

options: Read as many lessons as possible before attempting any practical work.
Learn a concept, apply it through appropriate practice, use feedback to identify gaps, and track growth over time.
Practice only when a lesson gives you a quiz.
Finish the curriculum once and rely on memory afterward.
quiz.explanation: Forge is designed around repeated movement between learning, applying, receiving feedback, and reviewing progress. The goal is skill development rather than simple lesson completion.

options: Debug Lab
Certificates
Academy Roadmap

summary: Forge is built around a Learn → Practice → Grow loop. Learn is where you study concepts and follow the curriculum. Practice is where you apply skills through tools such as Playground, Debug Lab, Whiteboard Mode, Projects, Quizzes, Flashcards, and Daily Challenges. Grow is where you review progress, mastery, and readiness. The goal is active skill development, not passive lesson completion.

title: Meet Your Browser DevTools
description: Learn what browser DevTools are, how to open them, and which panel to reach for when you need to inspect a page, investigate an error, or understand a network request.
mastery: Learner can open DevTools in their browser, identify the Elements, Console, Network, and Sources panels, explain what each panel is useful for, and choose an appropriate panel for a simple frontend problem.
learningObjectives: Explain what browser DevTools are and why frontend engineers use them.
Open DevTools using a keyboard shortcut or the browser's Inspect option.
Identify the Elements, Console, Network, and Sources panels and describe the kind of problem each can help investigate.
Choose the most appropriate DevTools panel for a simple layout, JavaScript, or network problem.

sections.text: Meet Your New Best Friend

Your browser comes with a set of tools built specifically for developers. They are called DevTools, short for Developer Tools. You do not install them separately, you do not need a special developer browser, and you do not need to earn the right to use them by suffering through three years of CSS.

DevTools lets you inspect a live webpage, see the HTML the browser is actually working with, inspect applied CSS, run JavaScript, investigate errors, watch network requests, and step through JavaScript execution. In professional frontend work, DevTools is not something you open only when everything has already caught fire. It is part of your normal workflow.
A useful mental model: your code editor shows you what you wrote. DevTools helps you inspect what the browser actually received, interpreted, changed, and ran.
Open DevTools

sections.title: Opening DevTools and Finding Your Way Around

steps.title: 1. Open a webpage
steps.description: Open any ordinary webpage in Chrome, Edge, or Firefox. Pick something you are comfortable looking at. You are about to inspect it, not break the internet.

steps.title: 2. Open DevTools
steps.description: Try F12 or Ctrl+Shift+I on Windows/Linux, or Cmd+Option+I on macOS. You can also right-click an element and choose Inspect. The exact menu wording can vary slightly between browsers.

steps.title: 3. Find the Elements panel
steps.description: Elements, sometimes called Inspector in Firefox, lets you inspect the live DOM and examine the HTML structure and CSS associated with selected elements.

steps.title: 4. Find the Console panel
steps.description: The Console provides a JavaScript environment connected to the current page and displays messages, warnings, and errors produced by the page. When something turns red, the browser is usually trying very hard to get your attention.

steps.title: 5. Find the Network panel
steps.description: Network shows requests made by the page, including documents, stylesheets, scripts, images, and API requests. You can inspect status codes, timing, request details, and responses.

steps.title: 6. Find the Sources panel
steps.description: Sources lets you inspect loaded source files and, when the browser has suitable source information, set breakpoints and step through JavaScript while it runs.

sections.text: The Four Panels You Need First

DevTools contains many features, but you do not need to memorize every tab today. Start with four panels: Elements, Console, Network, and Sources. These give you a foundation for inspecting structure and styles, investigating JavaScript problems, understanding requests, and tracing code execution.

sections.title: Which Panel Should You Reach For?
sections.description: Elements → inspect DOM structure and CSS. Console → inspect messages, warnings, errors, and run JavaScript experiments. Network → inspect requests, responses, status codes, and timing. Sources → inspect loaded source files and debug JavaScript with breakpoints.

sections.text: Elements: What Does the Browser Have?

The Elements panel shows the live DOM tree. This is important because the page you inspect is not necessarily identical to the HTML file you originally wrote. JavaScript can add, remove, or change elements after the page loads.

You can select an element and inspect its structure, classes, attributes, and applied styles. You can also make temporary edits in DevTools and immediately see the result. Those edits are useful experiments, but they do not permanently rewrite your source code.

Common mistake: changing CSS in DevTools and thinking you just fixed the application. You fixed the browser's current copy. Reload the page and your temporary experiment is gone. DevTools is an excellent laboratory, not your production deployment pipeline.
Console: What Is the Browser Saying?

The Console is where you can inspect JavaScript messages and errors and run small JavaScript expressions against the current page. It is often one of the first places to look when an interaction suddenly stops working.

Try entering the expressions above in the Console. The first asks JavaScript to evaluate an expression. The second writes a message to the Console. You are not building an application here; you are getting comfortable asking the browser questions.
Network: What Is Going Across the Wire?
The Network panel records requests made by the page. You can use it to see which resources were requested, whether they succeeded, how long they took, and what kind of response came back.

Remember your previous lessons. You already learned that browsers communicate with servers using requests and responses. The Network panel gives you a place to actually see that conversation happening.
If you open Network after a page has already loaded and see almost nothing useful, reload the page while the panel is open. The network log is not a time machine.
Sources: Where Is the Code Running?

The Sources panel lets you inspect source files loaded by the page and, when appropriate, pause JavaScript execution with breakpoints. Instead of guessing what a function is doing, you can stop the program and inspect what is happening at a particular point.

sections.title: You do not need to master Sources today
sections.subtitle: Know what it is for
sections.content: Sources becomes much more useful once you know JavaScript well enough to understand execution flow and debugging. For now, remember its main job: inspecting source code and helping you pause and trace JavaScript execution. Forge will return to this skill when the curriculum reaches deeper debugging.

sections.text: Try It Yourself

Open DevTools on a familiar webpage. Start in Elements and select something visible on the page. Find the Console and run 2 + 2. Open Network and reload the page. Finally, open Sources and locate at least one loaded script or source file.

sections.label: Open DevTools on a real webpage and identify the Elements, Console, Network, and Sources panels. Then explain which panel you would use first for a CSS/layout problem, a JavaScript error, a failed API request, and a problem where you need to pause JavaScript execution.
sections.hint: Think: structure and styling, JavaScript messages, network communication, and stepping through code.

sections.text: Forge Check

You do not need to memorize every DevTools feature. Your first win is knowing where to look. If a page looks wrong, investigate Elements. If JavaScript is complaining, check Console. If data is not arriving, inspect Network. If you need to stop code and see what it is doing, move toward Sources.
That is enough for today. In the next lesson, we will stop touring DevTools and start using one of its panels to inspect and change a live page.

quiz.explanation: The Network panel lets you inspect requests, status codes, request details, timing, and responses, making it the appropriate first place to investigate a failed network request.

summary: Browser DevTools is a built-in suite for inspecting and debugging live web pages. Elements helps investigate DOM structure and CSS, Console helps investigate JavaScript messages and errors, Network helps inspect requests and responses, and Sources helps inspect source files and debug JavaScript execution.

title: Inspecting HTML with Elements
description: Use the Elements panel to inspect the live DOM, understand which HTML the browser is actually using, and experiment with HTML and CSS without changing your source code.
mastery: Learner can use the Elements panel to select a visible element, identify its place in the live DOM, inspect its attributes and applied styles, make a temporary HTML or CSS change, and explain why that change does not permanently modify the source code.
learningObjectives: Explain what the Elements panel shows and how it relates to the live DOM.
Select a visible element on a webpage and inspect its HTML structure, attributes, and applied CSS.
Make a temporary HTML or CSS change in DevTools and observe the result.
Explain the difference between changing the live page in DevTools and changing the application's source code.

sections.text: Now We Actually Inspect Something
In the last lesson, you met DevTools and learned what its main panels are for. Now we are going to use one of them for real: Elements.

The Elements panel lets you inspect the live DOM, which is the browser's current representation of the page structure. You can select an element, see where it sits inside that structure, inspect its attributes, and see which CSS rules are affecting it.

Your HTML file is the recipe you wrote. The live DOM is the meal the browser actually prepared. They are closely related, but JavaScript can change the DOM after the page loads, so the live version can look different from the original source.
Find an Element

steps.title: 1. Open a webpage
steps.description: Use a page you already have open or choose a simple site you can inspect comfortably.

steps.title: 2. Open Elements
steps.description: Open DevTools and select the Elements panel. You should see a tree of HTML elements representing the current page.

steps.title: 3. Use the element picker
steps.description: Choose the element picker tool, usually shown as a small cursor or target icon, then move over something visible on the page. Click an element to jump directly to its place in the DOM.

steps.title: 4. Read the structure
steps.description: Look at the selected element and its parent and child elements. Notice how the browser represents nested HTML as a tree rather than as a flat list.

steps.title: 5. Inspect attributes
steps.description: Look for attributes such as class, id, href, src, or aria-* values. These are part of the selected element's current markup.

steps.title: 6. Inspect the styles
steps.description: Use the Styles area to see which CSS declarations apply to the selected element, including which rules win when multiple rules compete.

sections.text: The DOM Is a Tree
Webpages are structured hierarchically. One element can contain another, which can contain another, and so on. DevTools visualizes that nesting as a tree.

In this example, main contains article, and article contains both h1 and p. When you inspect the page in Elements, you can expand and collapse those relationships just like opening folders on your computer.

When debugging layout or structure, do not only ask 'What should this element look like?' Ask 'Where does this element live in the DOM, and what is around it?' A surprising number of CSS problems begin with the wrong ancestor, child, or nesting relationship.
Edit the Live Page
Here is where DevTools starts feeling a little magical. You can temporarily edit the HTML or CSS of a live page and immediately see the result.

Change a heading's text. Add a class. Disable a CSS declaration. Change a color. Adjust padding. These experiments are extremely useful because you can test a hypothesis before touching your source code.

You can add rules like these in the Styles panel and immediately observe the effect. This is one of the fastest ways to answer questions such as 'Is this selector actually applying?' or 'Would more padding solve this layout problem?'
Important: DevTools edits are temporary. Reload the page and your experiment will usually disappear. Congratulations—you have just discovered one of the safest places to break a website on purpose.
Live DOM vs Source Code

The live DOM is what the browser is currently working with. Your source code is what exists in the project files. They can differ because JavaScript can create elements, remove elements, change attributes, and update text after the page loads.

sections.title: Why this matters when debugging
sections.subtitle: Inspect what exists, not what you remember writing
sections.content: A common debugging mistake is looking only at the source code and assuming the browser must be using exactly the same structure. When a page behaves strangely, inspect the live DOM. A script may have changed it, a framework may have rendered a different structure than you expected, or another CSS rule may be affecting the element.

sections.text: Watch the Styles Panel

When you select an element, DevTools shows the CSS rules that apply to it. Some declarations may be crossed out because another rule wins. Some styles may come from inherited properties. This gives you a direct view into why the browser is styling the element the way it is.

You do not need to master CSS specificity today. Just notice the relationship: the element is one piece of the DOM, and the Styles panel shows the rules currently affecting how that piece is presented.
Practice: Inspect, Change, Reset

Pick a visible heading, button, or card on a real webpage. Inspect it in Elements. Identify its tag, one attribute, and one CSS rule affecting it. Then make one temporary change—for example, change its color or padding. Finally, reload the page and verify that your change disappeared.

sections.title: Inspect the Live DOM
sections.instructions: Select the example card mentally as if you were using the Elements panel. Change its text, then change its padding and background color. Pay attention to the difference between the HTML structure and the CSS that controls presentation. Finally, reload the simulation to see that the changes were temporary.

sections.label: Inspect a real webpage using Elements. Select one visible element, identify its tag and one attribute, identify one applied CSS rule, make one temporary change, and explain why that change does not permanently modify the site's source code.
sections.hint: Think: live DOM, attributes, styles, temporary browser changes, and source files.

sections.text: Forge Check

The important habit is not memorizing where every DevTools button lives. It is learning to inspect reality instead of guessing. When a button is mysteriously 12 pixels too far to the left, do not negotiate with it emotionally. Select it, inspect the DOM, inspect its styles, and find out what the browser is actually doing.
In the next lesson, we move from the page itself to the browser's Console, where you will start asking JavaScript questions and reading the browser's answers.

exercises.title: Inspect and Experiment
exercises.brief: Open a real webpage and use Elements to inspect one visible element. Record its tag, one attribute, and one CSS rule affecting it. Make one temporary HTML or CSS change, observe the result, then reload and confirm that the change is gone.

quiz.question: What does the Elements panel primarily let you inspect?
options: Only files stored on the server
The live DOM structure and the HTML and CSS associated with selected elements
Only JavaScript execution timing
Only network request headers
quiz.explanation: Elements lets you inspect the current DOM and examine the HTML structure and styles associated with selected elements.

quiz.question: You change a button's background color in the Elements/Styles panel, then reload the page. The color returns to its original value. Why?
options: DevTools can only change colors for one second.
The server rejects all CSS changes automatically.
The DevTools edit changed the live page temporarily rather than the application's source code.
The browser cannot display edited CSS.
quiz.explanation: DevTools edits modify the current page running in the browser. They are useful experiments, but they do not automatically change the source files in the project.

quiz.question: Why is inspecting the live DOM useful when debugging a page?
options: Because the live DOM is always identical to the original source code.
Because JavaScript and other runtime behavior can change the page after the original HTML was loaded.
Because CSS is stored inside the DOM and cannot exist elsewhere.
Because DevTools automatically fixes incorrect HTML.
quiz.explanation: The live DOM represents the browser's current document structure. Scripts can add, remove, or change elements after the initial HTML is loaded, so inspecting the live result can reveal what the browser is actually working with.

summary: The Elements panel lets you inspect the live DOM, examine attributes and applied CSS, and make temporary changes to experiment with a page. Those edits are useful for testing ideas and diagnosing problems, but they do not replace changing the application's actual source code.

resources.label: Chrome DevTools — Inspect and debug DOM nodes

Why are DevTools style changes temporary?
